metadata.title: False Weights and Short Measure
metadata.description: Calculate a dishonest seller’s actual margin when the amount delivered differs from the amount charged.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop the commercial relationship step by step, explain why each rate uses its base, show intermediate amounts, check signs and units, then practice transfer with misconception-specific retries.
metadata.sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 12 “Profit and Loss,” printed pages 374–425. Approved scope: Model the actual quantity bought, sold, and paid for when a scale, metre, or weight is inaccurate. Separate the nominal CP/SP per stated unit from the true amount transferred; derive effective gain/loss from actual currency and true quantity rather than memorizing a formula alone. Cover selling at claimed CP, claiming a stated gain/loss while short-weighing, and compounding an ordinary margin with a short measure. Check units and test a simple 1 kg or 1 m base. Use solved examples 18–20 and related objective patterns.

content.text: False Weights and Short Measure: Calculate a dishonest seller’s actual margin when the amount delivered differs from the amount charged. We establish the model, explain each step, and practice with targeted feedback.
A short measure changes the amount of goods delivered, even if the displayed price is unchanged. Compare the seller’s receipt with the true cost of the quantity actually handed over.
If a kilogram costs the seller ₹100 and the seller charges ₹100 while delivering only 960 g, true cost of delivered goods is ₹96. Profit is ₹4 on ₹96, so actual gain is 4⅙%.
The denominator remains the seller’s actual cost, ₹96. It is not ₹100 because that is the nominal unit cost, not the cost of the amount delivered.
For a short weight that is y% below one kilogram, delivered quantity factor is 1−y/100. At nominal cost price, the receipt corresponds to one full kg while actual cost is only that fraction.
Thus the gain rate for a seller charging a full-kilogram cost is y/(100−y)×100%. For y=4%, this is 4/96×100%=4⅙%.
If the seller also advertises an ordinary x% gain on the nominal kilogram, receipt factor is 1+x/100 while actual delivered cost factor is 1−y/100. Calculate actual profit from their difference.
For example, a 10% stated gain with a 20% short weight means receipt=1.10C and actual cost=0.80C. Gain=0.30C on actual cost 0.80C, a 37.5% true gain.
A short measure can also be used when buying. Keep track of who receives the smaller amount and who pays the stated amount; buying fraud and selling fraud reverse the advantage.
A faulty two-pan balance may deliver an overweight or underweight quantity depending on which side carries the goods and which carries the reference weight.
Set a simple nominal base: let the price of one true kilogram be ₹100 or the cost per gram be ₹1. Calculate the actual amount exchanged before taking a rate.
False metre scales work the same way. If a seller charges for one metre but delivers 90 cm, compare charge with the true cost of 90 cm.
Do not apply the shortcut without checking its assumptions: the stated price is per nominal unit, the weight error is a fraction of the true unit, and gain percent is measured on actual CP.
If the problem says the seller sells at a stated loss and uses short weights, represent nominal receipt and actual quantity separately. The final result may still be a gain.
Use units throughout: grams delivered, rupees charged, rupees per kilogram. This catches the common error of comparing money for 1 kg with cost of 960 g as if they were equal quantities.
Check the direction: a seller who charges for more goods than delivered should improve profit, all else equal. A larger short measure should increase that effect.
